text: A quick honesty note before anything else: this environment can't execute a real IBM Quantum job, so this lesson illustrates what a noisy real-hardware-style result looks like using a simulated noise model applied to a known circuit — not a literal result pulled from an actual backend. The point isn't the specific numbers; it's learning to recognize the real signature of hardware noise when you see it.

Start from the same Bell-state circuit used throughout this course. On a noiseless simulator, the only two possible outcomes are 00 and 11, each with exact probability 0.5. 01 and 10 have exact probability 0 — there's no path through this ideal circuit that produces a mismatched pair.

Real hardware doesn't implement gates perfectly. Using a depolarizing noise model at p equals 0.05 on the entangling gate — a more pronounced, realistic noise level — the exact probabilities work out to 0.4875 for 00 and 11, and 0.0125 for 01 and 10. 00 and 11 are still by far the dominant outcomes, each losing a small amount of probability. But 01 and 10, exactly zero in the ideal case, now each pick up a small, nonzero share. That shift is the entire signature of the noise.

A real seeded draw from these exact probabilities at 4096 shots gives something like 00: 2005, 11: 2003, 01: 35, 10: 53. Compare this to the clean simulator pattern from earlier in the course, where 01 and 10 always came back at exactly zero. Here they don't — 35 and 53 counts, roughly in line with the 0.0125 probability each was assigned, allowing for ordinary sampling variation on top of the noise itself.

Here's the practical takeaway that matters more than any specific number: on real hardware, you should expect to see nonzero counts on outcomes that your circuit's ideal math says are impossible. That is not evidence your circuit is wrong, not a bug in your code, and not something to fix by rewriting the circuit — it's the expected fingerprint of genuine gate error and readout error accumulating on physical qubits.

The question to ask isn't what you did wrong — it's whether this noise level is consistent with what you'd expect from this backend, and whether your results are still usable or need error mitigation to clean them up. That question is exactly what Chapter 7 is about.

Next lesson closes this chapter with the practical, career-relevant constraint underneath all of it: you almost certainly have a limited amount of real hardware access, and how you spend it is a real engineering decision.
